title: When digitalization fuels divergence: the Digital Matthew Effect and regional innovation divide in Europe
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine whether digitalization promoted regional convergence across the European Union between 2015 and 2023 or reinforced a persistent Digital Matthew Effect. This study focuses on how regional Digital Intangible Capital, combining research capacity, specialized human capital, digital adoption and institutional maturity, relates to economic performance and whether digital advantages spread beyond established innovation hubs. Design/methodology/approach The study analyzes 233 EU NUTS-2 regions in 2015, 2019 and 2023. It integrates New Economic Geography with a technological condensation framework, constructs an entropy-weighted Digital Intangible Capital Index and estimates time-stratified Spatial Durbin Models. Robustness is assessed using alternative index weights and k-nearest-neighbor matrices ranging from k = 2 to k = 15. Findings The results indicate a persistent Digital Matthew Effect and a stable core-periphery structure. Although aggregate dispersion in the index declines, this largely reflects convergence in basic digital access, while innovation-intensive capabilities remain concentrated. Direct effects of Digital Intangible Capital are positive and significant, whereas indirect spatial effects remain statistically insignificant across years and specifications. Research limitations/implications The analysis relies on three cross-sectional snapshots and therefore identifies conditional spatial associations rather than causal effects. Missing regional observations required hierarchical imputation, which may reduce variation in some indicators. Future research should use panel and micro-level data to identify knowledge-diffusion mechanisms more precisely. Practical implications EU Cohesion Policy should complement infrastructure investment with support for specialized skills, R&D capacity, institutional quality and durable cross-regional innovation networks. Social implications Persistent concentration of digital innovation may deepen regional inequality, brain drain and unequal access to high-value employment and wealth creation. Originality/value The study combines spatial econometrics, multidimensional intangible-capital measurement and a technological condensation framework to distinguish local returns from network-mediated effects and demonstrate that the identified pattern is robust to alternative weighting and spatial specifications.

title: Voluntary Channeling and the Limitations to Financial Redistribution in the Special Drawing Rights System
abstract: Abstract The idea of “voluntary channeling” of Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) has gained prominence as a potential mechanism for providing concessionary financing to emerging market economies and low-income developing countries. This article critically assesses the redistributive potential of voluntary channeling by analyzing the SDR system as a web of interlocking balance sheets governed by idiosyncratic accounting rules established in the late Bretton Woods era. We distinguish three prevailing interpretations of voluntary channeling: direct transfers of SDR holdings between countries, transfers to development banks, and lending to IMF-sponsored Trusts. Using balance-sheet methodology, we show that using SDR holdings always entails perpetual interest payments and therefore cannot be costless for donors. Only lending SDRs via IMF Trusts can shield donors from direct costs, as contributors are compensated at the SDR interest rate. However, the subsidy required to make Trust lending concessionary must be sourced elsewhere and has often also been financed through IMF surcharges and cross-subsidization from indebted emerging economies. As a result, voluntary channeling tends to redistribute resources within the Global South while allowing advanced economies to avoid meaningful wealth transfers. One promising idea for reform to overcome these shortcomings entails turning SDR allocations into tradable liabilities.

title: Visual trust signals in digital financial marketplaces: eye-tracking evidence from verification badges
abstract: Purpose This study examines when a platform-issued verification badge affects consumer choice in a high-uncertainty digital financial marketplace. Integrating signaling theory and attention-based choice research, it distinguishes signal assignment, item-card visual consideration, post-task self-reported badge noticing, and hypothetical selection. Design/methodology/approach A controlled eye-tracking experiment involved 60 participants. Each participant viewed 10 NFT listings, five randomly assigned a badge within the participant's choice set, and selected three listings for hypothetical purchase. Item-card fixation, time to first fixation, fixation count and selection were analyzed using participant and item fixed effects and a Cox model. Findings Badged item-cards were fixated in 83.3% of observations, compared with 35.7% for unbadged item-cards. Among cards with an observed first fixation, badge assignment was associated with an approximately 1.47-s earlier first fixation. Hypothetical selection rates were 42.3% for badged listings and 17.7% for unbadged listings. The estimated badge-selection relationship was substantially stronger among participants who reported clearly noticing the badge. The gaze measures concern the full item-card rather than direct badge-icon fixation, and noticing was not experimentally manipulated. Originality/value By combining randomized cue assignment, eye-tracking, and item-level choice data, the study provides process-level evidence consistent with an attention-gated signaling account. It extends digital trust-cue research from service-level adoption to micro-level choice while bounding the evidence to hypothetical selection in a controlled interface.

title: Urban pavement condition assessment with hyperspectral remote sensing: a case study of concrete pavements
journal: Built Environment Project and Asset Management
abstract: Purpose Concrete pavements are vital to transportation infrastructure, yet their timely condition assessment remains a major challenge because conventional monitoring techniques, such as visual inspection and the Pavement Condition Index (PCI), are often costly, time-consuming, and spatially constrained. This study examines the applicability and reliability of hyperspectral remote sensing as a non-destructive and scalable method for assessing the condition of concrete pavements. Design/methodology/approach A total of 36 field spectrometer data and Airborne Visible and Infrared Imaging Spectrometer–Next Generation imagery were integrated to analyze concrete pavements. Reflectance data from normal and cracked surfaces were compared to identify diagnostic absorption features and quantify spectral indices, including normalized indices, near-infrared (NIR), and shortwave infrared (SWIR) ratios. Findings The analysis revealed distinct absorption bands at approximately 478 nm, 1,060 nm, and 2,207 nm, corresponding to iron oxide, hygroscopic water, and clay minerals, respectively. Compared with normal surfaces, cracked pavements exhibited a 10–15% decrease in overall reflectance and a significant increase in spectral indices. Regression analysis demonstrated a strong field-to-image correlation (R2 = 0.77–0.81), confirming methodological reliability. Research limitations/implications The study is limited to one urban context; validation is required across diverse regions, materials, and traffic conditions. Practical implications The approach provides a robust and cost-effective method for assessing pavement conditions. Combining field spectroscopy with airborne hyperspectral imagery enables the early detection of deterioration and scalable monitoring to support innovative infrastructure management. Originality/value This research presents a novel framework for monitoring concrete pavements in India, demonstrating the potential of hyperspectral remote sensing to enhance large-scale urban road assessments.

title: Transformación digital y reconfiguración institucional en el Poder Judicial peruano: tensiones, avances y límites del Expediente Judicial Electrónico
abstract: La transformación digital del sistema judicial peruano, lejos de limitarse a la incorporación de herramientas tecnológicas, configura un proceso de reconfiguración institucional cuya complejidad se manifiesta en la tensión constante entre innovación normativa, dinámicas organizacionales heredadas y condicionamientos sociopolíticos específicos. A través del estudio del Expediente Judicial Electrónico (EJE), se examinan críticamente las trayectorias de implementación tecnológica y los marcos institucionales que interactúan con las políticas de digitalización, identificando patrones de fragmentación estructural que desafían los supuestos de eficiencia y modernización frecuentemente asociados a estos procesos. Los hallazgos apuntan a una digitalización paradójica, donde la proliferación de iniciativas aisladas, la desarticulación entre actores institucionales, las debilidades en ciberseguridad y la persistencia de marcos normativos precarios configuran un escenario de vulnerabilidad estructural. En este contexto, se observa cómo las tensiones entre diseño formal y prácticas cotidianas reflejan no solo resistencias organizacionales, sino también una fragilidad de la arquitectura institucional que sostiene el proceso. Lejos de constituir una narrativa de éxito lineal, la experiencia peruana revela una modernización fragmentada en el que los avances técnicos coexisten con déficits de legitimidad, sostenibilidad y equidad, poniendo de relieve la necesidad de un enfoque sistémico que trascienda lo meramente instrumental e integre dimensiones de gobernanza, justicia social y resiliencia institucional.

title: The genetic profile of B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia diagnosed in Pretoria, South Africa: A 10-year retrospective study
journal: Journal of the Colleges of Medicine of South Africa
abstract: Background: B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (B-ALL) comprises genetically distinct subtypes with important prognostic implications. South African data suggest a different genetic landscape to other geographic regions, with a higher frequency of t(1;19). This study aimed to describe the genetic profile of B-ALL diagnosed at a South African tertiary haematology laboratory over a 10-year period. Methods: In this retrospective, descriptive study, all B-ALL cases (2014–2023) recorded in flow cytometry and cancer registries were identified. Demographic and laboratory data, including immunophenotypic and genetic findings, were extracted from the laboratory information system. Genetic work-up included karyotyping, a routine fluorescence in situ hybridisation panel: KMT2A rearrangement, t(1;19), t(12;21) and t(9;22), and real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction where available. Results: A total of 173 patients were included (54.9% male; 75.7% < 19 years). Genetic testing was requested in 146 cases (84.4%), with definitive results in 115 (78.8%). Among informative cases, t(1;19) was most frequent (26.1%), followed by t(9;22) (12.2%), t(12;21) (10.4%), high hyperdiploidy (9.6%), KMT2A rearrangement (7.0%) and hypodiploidy (0.9%). The t(1;19) translocation predominated in paediatric patients, while t(9;22) was more common in adults. Both t(12;21) and KMT2A rearrangements were restricted to patients < 19 years. Conclusion: This cohort demonstrates a high frequency of t(1;19) and age-specific variation in B-ALL genetic subtypes, suggesting a distinct regional genetic profile. Expanded diagnostic testing and multicentre African studies are needed to refine risk stratification and guide context-appropriate care. Contribution: This study provides data on the distribution of selected genetic subtypes of B-ALL in a South African population, identifying differences in subtype frequency and age distribution that may inform regional diagnostic strategies and risk-directed care.

title: The Bosadi-Salutogenic framework: culturally embedded identity as a personal resource for work engagement among Black South African women in middle management
abstract: The dominance of Euro-American frameworks in industrial and organizational psychology has rendered culturally embedded work experiences largely invisible. While foundational models such as the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) framework elegantly illuminate universal engagement mechanisms across diverse contexts, occupational health literature has traditionally paid less attention to how intersecting racialized and gendered identities shape occupational well-being in postcolonial settings. This conceptual paper addresses this contextual gap by examining the organizational position of Black women in South African middle management, a group navigating unique structural tensions rooted in historical exclusion and contemporary marginalization. Responding to calls for disciplinary decolonization, I propose an integrated Afrocentric framework that brings Bosadi theorization into conversation with salutogenic principles. Specifically, I argue that Bosadi identity functions are not merely as a demographic marker but as a culturally embedded personal resource that shapes how job demands are interpreted, managed, and made meaningful. By positioning identity as an analytic resource rather than a contextual variable, the framework extends the JD-R model’s explanatory power to account for culturally specific modes of resilience and meaning-making. The paper concludes by outlining theoretical contributions to organizational psychology and offering directions for empirical research, including methodological considerations for studying culturally situated work experiences. This work aims to support the development of organizational practices that are genuinely responsive to the lived realities of historically marginalized women.

title: Two hands of green innovation: how digital social responsibility fuels circular economy practices and net-zero outcomes
journal: International Journal of Productivity and Performance Management
abstract: Purpose This study investigates how digital social responsibility contributes to sustainability transformation by examining its effects on green innovation, circular economy practices, and net-zero-based green performance. Drawing on Stakeholder Theory and Dynamic Capabilities Theory, the study explores the mechanisms through which digitally enabled responsibility shapes innovation-based environmental outcomes. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative research design is employed, using survey data collected from technology-based firms in Vietnam. Structural equation modeling is applied to test the proposed relationships among digital social responsibility, exploitative and exploratory green innovation, circular economy practices, and net-zero-based green performance. Findings The results indicate that digital social responsibility is positively associated with exploratory green innovation but not with exploitative green innovation. Exploratory green innovation is positively associated with circular economy practices, and both green innovation and circular economy practices are positively associated with net-zero-based green performance. In addition, digital social responsibility shows significant positive associations with both circular economy practices and net-zero-based green performance. Originality/value This study advances digital sustainability literature by redefining digital social responsibility as a digital sustainability orchestration capability that links stakeholder engagement with dynamic capability formation. It further reveals how digital social responsibility-driven exploratory innovation translates into circular-economy practices and net-zero-based green performance in emerging-economy technology firms, offering new process-level insights into the digital-enabled sustainability transformation.
